title: Sachin Yadav Failed to Breach 80 Metres in Rome. Sri Lanka's Pathirage Threw 92.62. No Indian Has Qualified for the Commonwealth Games.
excerpt: India's javelin heir struggled to 79.18 metres on his Diamond League debut while a 23-year-old Sri Lankan became only the fourth Asian to break the 90-metre barrier.
body:
India's javelin programme, once the country's proudest export to world athletics, is facing an uncomfortable reckoning. At the Rome Diamond League on Thursday night, Sachin Yadav — the man tasked with carrying Indian javelin into a new era — finished eighth on his debut, failing to breach the 80-metre barrier with a best throw of 79.18 metres. As he trudged off the Stadio Olimpico infield, Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage was busy rewriting history.

Pathirage, a 23-year-old former medium-pace bowler who took up javelin full-time in 2017, produced a stunning 92.62-metre throw on his second attempt of the evening. The distance fell just 35 centimetres short of Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem's Asian record and Olympic gold medal-winning mark set at the Paris 2024 Games. It was the fourth-best throw ever recorded by an Asian, and it shattered the 20-year-old meet record of 90.34 metres set by Norway's Andreas Thorkildsen in 2006.

In one throw, Pathirage had become only the fourth Asian to surpass the 90-metre barrier, joining Chinese Taipei's Cheng Chao-Tsun, India's Neeraj Chopra, and Nadeem. He now holds the top two leading throws in men's javelin this year. Former world champion Anderson Peters of Grenada was a distant second with 83.91 metres.

## India's Heir Apparent Struggles

Sachin Yadav's series in Rome told a story of regression, not progression. After an opening foul, he registered 79.18 metres on his second attempt — which remained his best of the evening. His graph went downward from there: 77.02, 76.62, and 75.54 metres in his final three attempts. He finished between Olympic medallists Julius Yego and Jakub Vadlejch.

This marked the second consecutive competition where the 26-year-old failed to cross the 80-metre mark. At the Federation Cup in Ranchi last month, he managed only 79.07 metres. For an athlete who finished fourth at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo with a personal best of 86.27 metres, the start to 2026 has been deeply concerning.

The result also means that no Indian javelin thrower has yet secured qualification for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, with the qualifying standard set at 82.61 metres. Sachin's next opportunity comes at the Indian Athletics Series in Ludhiana on June 13, where the Athletics Federation of India has offered athletes a final chance to breach the threshold.

## The Neeraj-Shaped Hole

The broader context makes India's position even more precarious. Neeraj Chopra, the Olympic and World Championship gold medallist whose 90.23-metre personal best once placed him at the pinnacle of Asian javelin, has not competed at all in 2026. He is currently training in Switzerland after injury and has not announced his season opener, though the Golden Spike meet in Ostrava on June 24 and the Neeraj Chopra Classic in Bengaluru on July 5 are potential return dates.

Until Chopra stepped onto the world stage, Indian javelin was a footnote in global athletics. He built the programme's credibility single-handedly. But the promise that his success would inspire a generation of Indian throwers has not materialised as hoped. Kishore Jena, India's second-best thrower, broke through with a silver at the 2023 Asian Games but has been inconsistent since.

## Asia's New Hierarchy

Pathirage's emergence has reshuffled the Asian pecking order in dramatic fashion. He has now surpassed Chopra's personal best and sits behind only Nadeem on the continent's all-time list. The Sri Lankan has competed frequently in India over the past two years — winning gold at the South Asian Athletics Championships in Ranchi and the Indian Open Continental Tour in Bhubaneswar — making his rise hard for Indian athletics to ignore.

The javelin landscape heading into the Glasgow Commonwealth Games and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya features Nadeem as the undisputed king, Pathirage as a new pretender, and India scrambling to remain relevant. For diaspora fans who watched Chopra's Paris gold with borrowed pride, the prospect of India sending no qualified javelin thrower to Glasgow would be a jarring reality check.

Sachin Yadav's talent is not in question. His fourth place at last year's World Championships proved he belongs at the highest level. But talent without consistency is a story Indian sport has told too many times. The clock is ticking, and the runway to Glasgow is getting shorter by the week.

*Sources: Olympics.com, The Bridge, RevSportz, IndiaSportsHub*
